title: From institutions to community: history and policy
blurb: Trace learning disability policy from long-stay hospitals to Building the Right Support, and use dynamic support registers and C(E)TRs to keep people out of hospital.
question: Marcus, 21, is autistic, has a learning disability and is on the local dynamic support register. His supported living placement is close to breaking down, and the commissioner suggests a specialist hospital 120 miles away. What should the community learning disability nurse do?

teach.body: For much of the twentieth century many people with learning disabilities lived in large long-stay hospitals, often far from family, segregated from community life. Policy has since moved towards ordinary homes in the community with the right support. In plain English: people with learning disabilities belong in their communities, not in institutions. Yet scandals show that institutional cultures can return wherever people are isolated.

The White Paper Valuing People set out the England policy definition of learning disability and four key principles: rights, independence, choice and inclusion. It introduced person-centred planning, health facilitation and health action plans, and Learning Disability Partnership Boards. Its message: people with learning disabilities should have the same opportunities and access to services as everyone else.

In 2011 BBC Panorama filmed staff abusing people with learning disabilities and autistic people at Winterbourne View, a private hospital. The government response, Transforming Care (2012), aimed to move people out of inpatient units into community support. Building the Right Support (2015) set out a national plan, and the 2022 action plan restated the target to halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 against March 2015. In 2019 abuse was exposed at Whorlton Hall.

teach.h: The inpatient target (Building the Right Support)
teach.caption: The target was missed. House of Commons Library SN07058.

teach.body: Each area keeps a dynamic support register (DSR) of people with a learning disability or autistic people at risk of admission to a mental health inpatient setting. Care (education) and treatment reviews (C(E)TRs) review care to avoid admission where possible and to challenge barriers to discharge. If someone is admitted without a community C(E)TR beforehand, a post-admission C(E)TR takes place within 28 days for adults and 14 days for children; if a community C(E)TR was held, the next review is six weeks after admission. The panel: a chair, an independent clinical expert and an independent expert by experience.
teach.cite: NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy and guide (2023)

steps.label: If admitted
steps.sub: C(E)TR 6 weeks after admission (or 28 days adult, 14 child if no community C(E)TR)

teach.caption: The Mental Health Act 2025 will put C(E)TRs and registers on a statutory footing for some people; those provisions are not yet in force.

teach.h: Scenario: Marcus and the distant hospital
teach.body: Marcus is on the DSR because he is at risk of admission. Before any move, the nurse asks for a community C(E)TR to look at what would keep him at home: an updated positive behaviour support plan, extra staffing, crisis support close to home. She involves Marcus and his family. Admission far from home risks isolation, loss of family contact and the closed-culture conditions seen at Winterbourne View.

teach.text: Order matters: Winterbourne View (2011) led to Transforming Care (2012), then Building the Right Support (2015) and its 2022 action plan. The halving target compared March 2024 with March 2015 and was missed. And the Mental Health Act 2025 changes are 'coming', not current law.

items: Valuing People 2001: rights, independence, choice, inclusion; person-centred planning; health action plans.
Winterbourne View 2011 -> Transforming Care 2012 -> Building the Right Support 2015 -> action plan 2022.
Target to halve inpatients by March 2024 missed: 2,055 in Feb 2025 (down 29%).
Closed cultures: isolation, few visitors, high restraint, poor leadership; speak up.
DSR and C(E)TRs: avoid admission; with no community C(E)TR, post-admission C(E)TR within 28 days (adults), 14 (children).

summary: You can now outline the move from long-stay hospitals to community support, connect Winterbourne View to Transforming Care and Building the Right Support, recognise closed-culture warning signs, and use dynamic support registers and C(E)TRs to avoid unnecessary admissions.

A.q: A nurse is preparing a teaching session on landmark reports. What did Death by Indifference (Mencap, 2007) describe?
options: Abuse filmed by undercover reporters at a private hospital
Six deaths of people with learning disabilities in NHS care
A confidential inquiry into every death in one region
The first national annual report of the LeDeR programme
A.why: Death by Indifference (Mencap, 2007) described six people with learning disabilities who died in NHS care; it led to the Healthcare for All inquiry (2008).

A.q: A family asks who sits on a care and treatment review (C(E)TR) panel. Which answer reflects NHS England policy?
options: The responsible clinician, a solicitor and the ward manager
Two doctors and an approved mental health professional
A chair, an independent clinical expert and an expert by experience
The GP, a social worker and one family member
A.why: NHS England's DSR and C(E)TR policy (2023): the panel is a chair, an independent clinical expert and an independent expert by experience.

whyNot.0: These people may contribute, but they are not the independent panel.
whyNot.1: Two doctors and an AMHP make up a Mental Health Act assessment, not a C(E)TR.
whyNot.3: These people may give views, but they are not the panel.

A.q: What is the purpose of a dynamic support register (DSR)?
options: To list people already detained under the Mental Health Act
To list people eligible for an annual health check at the GP
To record the reasonable adjustments a person needs for NHS care
To identify people at risk of admission to an inpatient setting
A.why: A DSR lists people with a learning disability or autistic people at risk of admission to a mental health inpatient setting, so support can be put in early.

whyNot.0: The register aims to prevent admission, not list detained patients.
whyNot.1: That is the GP learning disability register.
whyNot.2: That is the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag.

B.q: Ola, 16, is autistic and has just been admitted to a mental health inpatient unit. No community C(E)TR was held before her admission. Under NHS England policy, when should her post-admission C(E)TR take place?
options: Within 14 days
Within 28 days
Within 72 hours
Within 6 weeks
B.why: NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy (2023) s14.2: where no community C(E)TR was held, the post-admission review is within 14 days (10 working days) for children and young people, 28 days for adults.

whyNot.1: 28 days is the timescale for adults.
whyNot.2: 72 hours is not the C(E)TR timescale.
whyNot.3: Six weeks after admission is the review point only when a community C(E)TR was held before admission, which did not happen here.

B.q: Healthcare for All (2008), the independent inquiry led by Sir Jonathan Michael, was a response to which report?
options: CIPOLD
Death by Indifference
Valuing People
Building the Right Support
B.why: Healthcare for All followed Mencap's Death by Indifference (2007).

whyNot.0: CIPOLD was published in 2013, after Healthcare for All.
whyNot.2: Valuing People was a 2001 White Paper, not a report Healthcare for All responded to.
whyNot.3: Building the Right Support came in 2015.

B.q: A colleague says the Mental Health Act 2025 has already made C(E)TRs a legal duty for detained autistic people and people with a learning disability. Which reply is accurate?
options: These provisions are in the Act but are not yet in force
These provisions came into force on Royal Assent in 2025
These provisions were removed before the Act was passed
These provisions apply to children now and to adults later
B.why: The 2025 Act (Royal Assent 18 December 2025) inserts statutory C(E)TR provisions, but they are prospective and not in force; NHS England policy currently governs C(E)TRs.

whyNot.1: Legislation.gov.uk shows these sections as prospective, not in force.
whyNot.2: They are in the Act as passed.
whyNot.3: They are not in force for any age group yet.

C.q: Marcus, 21, is autistic, has a learning disability and is on the dynamic support register. His placement is close to breaking down. The commissioner suggests a specialist hospital 120 miles away. What should the community learning disability nurse do?
options: Agree to admission, as the placement is breaking down
Request a community C(E)TR to plan support near home
Wait for the post-admission review to plan discharge
Ask for a Mental Health Act assessment to authorise it
C.why: Building the Right Support and NICE NG93 aim for intensive support in the community close to home. A community C(E)TR looks at what would avoid admission.

whyNot.0: Admission far from home should not be the default response to placement breakdown.
whyNot.2: Waiting until after admission misses the chance to avoid it.
whyNot.3: A Mental Health Act assessment is for detention, not a route to plan support.

C.q: Kwame, 32, has a learning disability and has lived on an inpatient unit for six years. His family live 200 miles away. Staff say he is 'settled'. Which action best reflects Transforming Care and Building the Right Support?
options: Accept a long stay, as he appears settled on the unit
Arrange video visits to reduce the effect of distance
Request transfer to an inpatient unit nearer his family
Raise discharge barriers at his C(E)TR and plan community support
C.why: C(E)TRs exist to challenge barriers to discharge. Policy aims for people to live in the community with the right support, close to home.

whyNot.0: Being 'settled' is not a reason to stay in hospital.
whyNot.1: Video calls help contact but leave him in hospital.
whyNot.2: A nearer unit is still inpatient care; the aim is community living.

C.q: Whorlton Hall (2019) exposed abuse similar to that found at Winterbourne View eight years earlier. Which lesson is most important for a newly registered nurse?
options: Abuse happens in private hospitals rather than NHS units
Units with fewer than 20 beds carry little risk of abuse
Closed cultures can recur, so raise concerns promptly
Regular CQC inspection is enough to prevent abuse
C.why: Abuse recurs where closed cultures develop: isolation, power imbalance, poor leadership. Nurses must recognise warning signs and speak up (NMC Code 16).

whyNot.0: Closed cultures can develop in any setting, NHS or private.
whyNot.1: Size does not protect against a closed culture.
whyNot.3: Inspection helps, but staff speaking up is essential between inspections.

reteach.title: A chain of scandal and response
reteach.question: Why does each big policy in learning disability seem to follow a scandal or a report of deaths?

blocks.body: Death by Indifference showed people dying from poor NHS care; Healthcare for All followed. Winterbourne View showed abuse in a hospital far from home; Transforming Care and Building the Right Support followed. Each reform aims to move care into the community and give people and families more voice.

blocks.text: Post-admission C(E)TR when no community C(E)TR was held: 28 days for adults, 14 days for children. After a community C(E)TR, the next review is six weeks after admission.

test.q: Which four principles did Valuing People (2001) set out?
options: Safety, care, protection and treatment
Rights, independence, choice and inclusion
Presence, choice, respect and competence
Empowerment, prevention, protection and partnership
test.why: Valuing People was built on four key principles: rights, independence, choice and inclusion.

whyNot.0: These reflect an older protective model of care.
whyNot.2: These are from O'Brien's five accomplishments.
whyNot.3: These are among the six safeguarding principles.

explain.body: Death by Indifference (2007, six deaths) led to Healthcare for All (2008). CIPOLD (2013) found people with learning disabilities died much younger and recommended a national mortality review, which became LeDeR.

test.q: Which programme grew out of the CIPOLD recommendation for a national mortality review body?
options: Transforming Care
STOMP
LeDeR
Valuing People
test.why: CIPOLD recommended a national learning disability mortality review body, which became LeDeR.

test.q: What was the Building the Right Support target for inpatients with a learning disability or autistic people?
options: Close all inpatient units by March 2020
Reduce numbers by a quarter by 2030
Halve numbers by March 2024 against March 2015
Halve the length of stay by March 2025
test.why: The 2022 action plan restated the target to halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 compared with March 2015.

whyNot.0: The target was a reduction, not closure of all units.
whyNot.1: The target was halving, by March 2024.
whyNot.3: The target concerned numbers of inpatients, not length of stay.

explain.body: Registers identify people at risk of admission. C(E)TRs avoid admission and challenge discharge barriers; if there was no community C(E)TR, the post-admission review is within 28 days (adults) or 14 days (children). Panel: chair, independent clinical expert, expert by experience.

test.q: Lewis, 30, has a learning disability and has just been admitted to an inpatient unit without a community C(E)TR beforehand. Within what time should his post-admission C(E)TR take place?
options: 28 days
7 days
14 days
3 months
test.why: For adults admitted without a community C(E)TR, the post-admission C(E)TR should take place within 28 days (20 working days).

whyNot.1: 7 days is not the policy timescale.
whyNot.2: 14 days applies to children and young people.
whyNot.3: 3 months is far longer than the policy allows.
